content: To further utilize the expertise and guidance of partners in planning and managing services, it is recommended that service units form an advisory committee comprising representatives from key collaborating partners. This committee can provide valuable support in areas such as planning, resource mobilization, monitoring, and evaluation, ultimately contributing to the effective functioning of prosthetics and orthotics services. The advisory committee should include user representatives, allowing them to influence the design and delivery of local services. This committee not only safeguards the mission of the program but also serves as a platform for raising awareness and promoting prosthetics and orthotics services. Financial management is a critical aspect of prosthetics and orthotics service provision. Service providers must manage expenses such as salaries, materials, consumables, rent, and utility bills. Funding sources may include government contributions, insurance payments, donations, or user fees, or a combination of these. Transparency and adherence to national financial practices are essential. Stock management and material procurement are equally important. The use of stock management software for procurement and disbursement should be considered. Human resource management in prosthetics and orthotics service units should align with the staff management procedures of the public, private, or NGO sectors in the country. Larger units or those integrated into broader service systems typically rely on specialized human resources departments. Key issues include defining and paying salaries, managing staff hours, and overseeing personnel insurance. Workforce planning, recruitment, continuous professional development (CPD), staff satisfaction, and retention are critical areas of focus. Annual performance appraisals should be conducted to evaluate individual employee productivity against agreed objectives. Data management is essential for prosthetics and orthotics service providers. Collecting data on service delivery and users supports planning, budgeting, monitoring, and evaluation at both local and national levels. Data should also be reviewed for quality management purposes. Consistent data collection and analysis provide insights into service success, such as productivity and outreach to target groups in various geographic areas. Anonymized data should be shared with central authorities for national-level analyses of needs and service availability. Integrated computerized systems and electronic clinical records are recommended for efficient data storage, management, and reporting. Quality management is a fundamental responsibility of prosthetics and orthotics service providers. This includes monitoring and improving the technical quality of prostheses and orthoses, as well as the overall quality of services provided to users. High-quality products should be durable, safe, functional, comfortable, aesthetically acceptable, and cost-effective. Services should be user-centered, accessible, polite, efficient, safe, and continuous, with appropriate follow-up and referrals. Quality management involves defining quality indicators and standards, measuring and monitoring quality, and taking corrective actions to address identified issues. This process is continuous and iterative, requiring regular reassessment and adjustment of quality indicators and standards as improvements are made. Feedback from users and caregivers should be systematically collected through surveys or focus group discussions to inform quality improvements. Service user representatives and organizations for disabled individuals can play a vital role in this process. In summary, effective management of financial, human, material, and data resources, combined with a robust quality assurance system, is essential for the successful delivery of prosthetics and orthotics services.
